title: Does More DNA Mean More Complex?

scenes.tts: The first film followed D N A sequence to proteins and traits. Does more D N A have to mean a more complex organism? To test that idea, we need counts from real chromosome sets, not guesses.
scenes.caption: The first film followed DNA sequence to proteins and traits. Does more DNA have to mean a more complex organism? To test that idea, we need counts from real chromosome sets, not guesses.
scenes.visual: Reuse the first film's dark world and COLOR MAP exactly: DNA sides BLUE; A/T YELLOW; C/G GREEN; gene TEAL; protein RED; trait GOLD; counts and axes GREY/WHITE. Carry in the gene-to-protein-to-trait path from the first film. Transform its DNA ladder into an empty bar-chart frame beside a human and onion cartoon. Put the spoken question across the top. No molecular structure.
scenes.narration: The first film followed DNA sequence to proteins and traits. Does more DNA have to mean a more complex organism? To test that idea, we need counts from real chromosome sets, not guesses.

scenes.visual: Keep the empty chart and human/onion cartoons moving gently. Add the title 'Does More DNA Mean More Complex?' for two seconds, then shrink it into the chart's question label.

scenes.tts: D N A amount means total base pairs in a full chromosome set. A base pair is a ladder rung. Scientists sequenced some living things and estimated others. These methods count D N A; they do not score complexity.
scenes.caption: DNA amount means total base pairs in a full chromosome set. A base pair is a ladder rung. Scientists sequenced some living things and estimated others. These methods count DNA; they do not score complexity.
scenes.visual: A large labelled block-ladder, marked 'schematic', fills the center. Its rungs tick through a counter, then compress into one horizontal bar. Above it, duplicate chromosome cartoons merge under the label 'one full chromosome set'. Split method tags into 'sequenced' and 'estimated'.
scenes.narration: DNA amount means total base pairs in a full chromosome set. A base pair is a ladder rung. Scientists sequenced some living things and estimated others. These methods count DNA; they do not score complexity.

scenes.tts: Watch each ladder become a counter, then a bar. Each bar shows published data for an organism. Every estimated value keeps its estimate label on screen.
scenes.caption: Watch each ladder become a counter, then a bar. Each bar shows published data for an organism. Every estimated value keeps its estimate label on screen.
scenes.visual: Transform three carried ladders into short horizontal bars. Expand into a full-height chart with room for all rows. Axis title: 'base pairs in one set (millions)'. Mark the graphic 'computed from lesson table'. Estimated rows receive a visible 'about / estimated' badge before any bar grows.
scenes.narration: Watch each ladder become a counter, then a bar. Each bar shows published data for an organism. Every estimated value keeps its estimate label on screen.

scenes.tts: The rows include a bacterium and fungus, then plant and animal examples. Every group represented here has D N A. That supports a careful claim about this table. It does not let this small set represent every living thing everywhere.
scenes.caption: The rows include a bacterium and fungus, then plant and animal examples. Every group represented here has DNA. That supports a careful claim about this table. It does not let this small set represent every living thing everywhere.
scenes.visual: Place large group icons down the left: bacterium, fungus, plant and animal. Slide the eight organism names beneath their group icons but keep bars hidden. A bracket labelled 'groups represented in this table' encloses them. Show the sample-size limit as a small neutral boundary, not a warning stamp.
scenes.narration: The rows include a bacterium and fungus, then plant and animal examples. Every group represented here has DNA. That supports a careful claim about this table. It does not let this small set represent every living thing everywhere.

scenes.tts: If amount ranked complexity, where should the human bar end compared with the onion bar? Make your prediction before either bar grows. Remember, this test compares a full chromosome set with a full chromosome set.
scenes.caption: If amount ranked complexity, where should the human bar end compared with the onion bar? Make your prediction before either bar grows. Remember, this test compares a full chromosome set with a full chromosome set.
scenes.visual: Keep only human and onion rows centered and large. Show their icons and empty bar tracks. Place the spoken question above them. At the left, keep a matched 'one set' bracket beside each row so chromosome-set scope remains visible.
scenes.narration: If amount ranked complexity, where should the human bar end compared with the onion bar? Make your prediction before either bar grows. Remember, this test compares a full chromosome set with a full chromosome set.

scenes.visual: Hold the full question and two empty bar tracks. A soft cursor moves from human to onion once. Do not reveal either value during the thinking pause.

scenes.tts: The human bar grows, but the onion bar continues far beyond it. The table's division appears on screen. The onion chromosome set has several times the human amount. A larger D N A total does not rank organism complexity.
scenes.caption: The human bar grows, but the onion bar continues far beyond it. The table's division appears on screen. The onion chromosome set has several times the human amount. A larger DNA total does not rank organism complexity.
scenes.visual: Grow the human bar to the table value, then grow onion on the same computed scale until it extends far beyond. Show the exact values and division only on screen: '16,400 ÷ 3,055 = 5.37 ≈ 5 times'. Keep onion's estimate badge. Do not speak the numbers.
scenes.narration: The human bar grows, but the onion bar continues far beyond it. The table's division appears on screen. The onion chromosome set has several times the human amount. A larger DNA total does not rank organism complexity.

scenes.tts: Now reveal every bar in data order. Rice extends beyond fruit fly, and onion extends beyond human. The pattern does not march from simpler to more complex. Total base count and organism complexity are different questions.
scenes.caption: Now reveal every bar in data order. Rice extends beyond fruit fly, and onion extends beyond human. The pattern does not march from simpler to more complex. Total base count and organism complexity are different questions.
scenes.visual: Restore all eight rows. Grow every bar on the full computed linear scale, then zoom into the crowded low end with a clearly relabelled axis. Animate a highlight from fruit fly to rice, then human to onion. Never label any organism 'simple', 'advanced', or 'more complex'.
scenes.narration: Now reveal every bar in data order. Rice extends beyond fruit fly, and onion extends beyond human. The pattern does not march from simpler to more complex. Total base count and organism complexity are different questions.

scenes.tts: Amount counts all base pairs, not only genes carrying protein instructions. It also does not tell which genes a cell uses. Sequence and gene use help explain traits. A total length cannot replace that information.
scenes.caption: Amount counts all base pairs, not only genes carrying protein instructions. It also does not tell which genes a cell uses. Sequence and gene use help explain traits. A total length cannot replace that information.
scenes.visual: Take one bar and transform it into a block strip labelled 'schematic—not to scale'. Add a teal gene bracket without implying a gene fraction. Duplicate the strip into skin and muscle cell cartoons, then glow different gene brackets in each. Keep the total strip length unchanged.
scenes.narration: Amount counts all base pairs, not only genes carrying protein instructions. It also does not tell which genes a cell uses. Sequence and gene use help explain traits. A total length cannot replace that information.

scenes.tts: Now both halves meet. D N A sequence helps shape traits; D N A amount does not rank organism complexity. The rule has scope. Amount here means base pairs in one chromosome set. Sequence helps through genes, proteins and gene use, and many traits also depend on the surroundings.
scenes.caption: Now both halves meet. DNA sequence helps shape traits; DNA amount does not rank organism complexity. The rule has scope. Amount here means base pairs in one chromosome set. Sequence helps through genes, proteins and gene use, and many traits also depend on the surroundings.
scenes.visual: Place the first film's gene-to-protein-to-trait path above the full bar chart. Show the exact guiding rule once between them. Under 'sequence', add small cautious arrows through gene and protein. Under 'amount', keep the 'one chromosome set' bracket. Add a surroundings icon beside the trait.
scenes.narration: Now both halves meet. DNA sequence helps shape traits; DNA amount does not rank organism complexity. The rule has scope. Amount here means base pairs in one chromosome set. Sequence helps through genes, proteins and gene use, and many traits also depend on the surroundings.

scenes.tts: These bars come from published lab studies, not field samples. Most rows come from one strain or sample. Several values are estimates. The human row is a set without Y, and onion uses an earlier estimate. Good evidence keeps limits attached.
scenes.caption: These bars come from published lab studies, not field samples. Most rows come from one strain or sample. Several values are estimates. The human row is a set without Y, and onion uses an earlier estimate. Good evidence keeps limits attached.
scenes.visual: Keep the chart visible. Slide in concise evidence tags beside the relevant rows: 'lab study', 'one strain/sample', 'estimated', '22 chromosomes + X; rounded', and 'earlier estimate'. Do not add names or dates. Each tag attaches to its row rather than floating as a list.
scenes.narration: These bars come from published lab studies, not field samples. Most rows come from one strain or sample. Several values are estimates. The human row is a set without Y, and onion uses an earlier estimate. Good evidence keeps limits attached.

scenes.tts: The films began with a strawberry and person sharing D N A parts. The answer is not a bigger ladder. Different base orders and different gene use can guide different proteins. D N A amount does not rank organism complexity.
scenes.caption: The films began with a strawberry and person sharing DNA parts. The answer is not a bigger ladder. Different base orders and different gene use can guide different proteins. DNA amount does not rank organism complexity.
scenes.visual: Return to the opening strawberry and student around a shared ladder labelled 'schematic'. Reorder their base blocks and glow different teal genes, then show different red protein blocks. Place two unequal amount bars below with 'schematic' and no winner labels. Fade everything except the two ideas.
scenes.narration: The films began with a strawberry and person sharing DNA parts. The answer is not a bigger ladder. Different base orders and different gene use can guide different proteins. DNA amount does not rank organism complexity.

scenes.visual: End card with one centered line only, large and high-contrast: 'DNA sequence helps shape traits; DNA amount does not rank organism complexity.' No title, logo, URL, subtitle, or smaller line.
